5-5.5.1 
Effective Corrosion Control. 
Effective corrosion control requires maintaining appropriate pH levels, plus adding 
maintenance dosages of chemical corrosion inhibitors. Chemical corrosion inhibitors 
form a protective film or barrier on the cooling system metal surfaces that have been 
cleaned prior to adding an initial high dosage of inhibitor. The initial high dosage of 
inhibitor passivates (protects) the metal. The appropriate dosage of corrosion inhibitor 
must be maintained continuously in the cooling water to ensure continuing protection. 
Table 5-11 shows examples of various passivation and maintenance dosage levels of 
corrosion inhibitors. Corrosion inhibitors are divided into three classes: cathodic, anodic, 
and general filmers. Corrosion inhibitors form a protective film on either the anode, the 
cathode, or over the entire metal surface. The types of corrosion inhibitors are 
described below. 
5-5.5.1.1 
Anodic Inhibitors. 
Anodic inhibitors form a protective film coating on the anodic metal (where the metal is 
lost) and thus directly control corrosion by preventing the reaction that results in 
corrosion. Any unprotected areas will corrode at a much faster rate than the protected 
areas, a factor that could result in pitting or localized attack of the unprotected areas. 
Examples of anodic inhibitors include orthophosphate, nitrite, and orthosilicates. Under 
certain conditions, molybdate can function as an anodic inhibitor. 


--- page 160 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
138 
5-5.5.1.2 
Cathodic Inhibitors. 
Cathodic inhibitors form a protective film coating of the cathodic metal (where metal is 
not lost) and thus indirectly prevent corrosion by interfering with the current flow 
required for the electrochemical reaction to proceed between the cathodic and anodic 
metals. The corrosion reaction rate is governed by the size and type of the cathode 
relative to the anode. Even when cathodic areas are not completely covered by the 
protective film, corrosion will occur, but usually more slowly and uniformly than when 
using anodic inhibitors alone. The occurrence of localized corrosion or pitting attack is 
greatly reduced. Examples of cathodic inhibitors include zinc salts, polyphosphates, and 
polysilicates. Under most conditions, molybdate will function as a cathodic inhibitor. 
5-5.5.1.3 
General Inhibitors. 
General inhibitors produce a protective film on the surfaces of all metals. These 
corrosion inhibitors are organic compounds, such as certain phosphonates, amines, and 
other nitrogen chemicals. They may be used in cooling water systems. 
5-5.5.1.4 
Corrosion Inhibitors for Specific Metals. 
Some corrosion inhibitors provide corrosion control for specific metals. The protection of 
copper and copper alloys requires the use of azoles, such as tolyltriazole (TTA), 
benzotriazole (BZT), and butylbenzo-thiazole, which can be added to the system 
separately from, or as part of a blend of, other treatment chemicals. 
5-5.5.1.5 
Galvanic or Crevice Corrosion. 
Control of galvanic or crevice corrosion is achieved primarily by engineering and 
mechanical design. These types of corrosion can also be partially controlled by physical 
and chemical considerations. A dielectric coupling (insulator), used to separate two 
different metallurgies, can help to prevent galvanic corrosion. From a chemical 
perspective, adjusting pH and using proper corrosion inhibitors will reduce corrosion. 
5-5.5.1.6 
Deposit Corrosion. 
Control of deposit corrosion requires maintaining deposit-free metal surfaces. This 
applies to any form of deposit, such as scale, biomass, corrosion products, or foulants. 
The occurrence of most types of deposits is prevented by dispersants, scale inhibitors, 
or biocides, along with the maintenance of adequate flow velocities. Routine, adequate 
cleaning of filters and tower sumps will help reduce deposits. 
5-5.5.1.7 
MIC. 
MIC is best prevented by stopping conditions that foster biological growth and by using 
an effective microbiological control program. A MIC prevention program includes 
adequate control (prevention) of deposits and fouling, avoidance of low-flow and dead-
leg conditions, and implementation of a consistently effective microbiological program 
(see paragraph 5-4.4).

An effective and complete cooling water treatment program addresses many factors, 
including those associated with compliance and safety, protection of equipment, and 
cost. Compliance and safety considerations are mandatory components of the program. 
Achieving or exceeding minimally acceptable equipment protection at the lowest 
possible cost is an advisable outcome for a well-designed program. The overall cost of 
the treatment program includes not only the cost of chemical treatment, but also the 
costs of water, disposal, manpower, and equipment. Development of an appropriate 
cooling water treatment program is dependent upon knowledge of both the specific 
equipment to be protected and the quality of the water to be used (source water and 
system water).

Equipment.

5-6.7.3 
Corrosion Test Coupons. 
When removing corrosion coupons, always note and record the visual appearance with 
regard to the presence of scale, rust, or biomass. Take photographs of the corrosion 
coupons. Submit (or evaluate) coupons for corrosion rate and for the type of corrosion 
that is occurring. 
5-6.7.4 
Inside Surface of Heat Exchanger Tubes. 
To effectively examine the inside (water-contacted) surfaces of heat exchanger tubes, a 
boroscope is needed because only a few inches of the interior can be seen visually 
using a flashlight. Scale deposits, typically hard and tightly adhered to the tube surface, 
range in color from white to gray or reddish, depending on the composition of the scale. 
No scale should be present. It is important to inspect heat exchanger tubes at least 
once per year. 
Fouling-type deposits may look similar to scale deposits. Unlike scale, these deposits 
usually adhere loosely to the tube surface. Biomass will appear slimy and feel slippery, 
and will usually adhere loosely. 
5-6.7.5 
Chiller Performance. 
Degradation of chiller performance or chiller efficiency may be a strong indication of 
scale or fouling problems in the chiller. If a reduction in chiller capacity occurs while 
cooling water is being cooled efficiently and within design parameters, then the chiller 
condenser section should be opened and examined. The chiller evaporator section may 
not contain water material scale but may be fouled with corrosion products. You should 
open and examine the chiller evaporator if chilled water could possibly be inadequately 
treated. 
5-6.7.6 
Cooling Tower Surfaces. 
Cooling towers made of galvanized steel should be examined for white rust or possible 
rusty surfaces that may indicate that the galvanizing is no longer present on the metal 
surfaces and the steel is rusting. Cooling towers constructed of wood should be 
examined for wood deterioration or decay. 
 
 


--- page 167 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
145 
5-7 
COOLING WATER SYSTEM START-UP AND LAYUP 
REQUIREMENTS. 
The startup of a new cooling water system requires special consideration. Proper 
cooling water system layup is also important, especially for chiller tube bundles or other 
heat exchange equipment. For a new cooling tower system, it is important to make sure 
that the equipment that contacts the cooling water is clean and properly protected from 
initial corrosion. Also, disinfection is needed to eliminate the presence of microbiological 
organisms that can cause corrosion, deposits, and growth of pathogenic organisms 
such as Legionella bacteria. Implementation of a proper layup process is critical to 
prevent corrosion and microbiological growth during stagnant water conditions. 
5-7.1 
Stand-by Conditions. 
The term “stand-by” is often applied to a chiller that is in rotation with other chillers on-
line. This stand-by period could be of varying duration, from a few days to a few weeks. 
Rotating chillers frequently is important for minimizing stagnant conditions that lead to 
under-deposit and MIC corrosion. It is good practice to run the recirculation pumps 
through a stand-by chiller for at least 15 minutes each day to minimize corrosion. A 
chiller that must be left on stand-by for an extended period of weeks without 
recirculation should be laid up wet or dry according to procedures described in 
paragraph 5-7.4. 
5-7.2 
Common Problems during Layup or Due to Improper Initial Start-up. 
Common problems that occur during layup or due to improper initial start-up include 
corrosion of tubes and transfer piping (sometimes to the point of failure), micro- 
biological growth with potential for MIC corrosion, and growth of pathogenic 
microorganisms. 
5-7.3 
Start-up of New Cooling Water Tower Systems. 
5-7.3.1 
Initial Cleaning. 
A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on 
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning 
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal 
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care 
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation 
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating 
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction 
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations 
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the 
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for 
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar 
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not 
apply. 
 
 


--- page 168 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
146 
5-7.3.2 
Cleaning and Passivation Procedures. 
In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that 
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling 
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These 
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional 
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water 
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust 
formation on galvanized surfaces and copper tubes. Galvanized steel can simply be 
passivated by exposure to highly aerated water and a phosphate or polysilicate 
treatment. This treatment forms a zinc corrosion inhibition layer, which is a natural, 
dense, adherent, and protective corrosion product film. High pH (above 8.5) produces 
unwanted white rust that is fragile and not protective against corrosion. The following 
procedures are recommended. 
5-7.3.2.1 
Hydrostatic Testing. 
Perform hydrostatic testing: 
a. Inspect and remove all debris. 
b. Fill the system with treated water and circulate. This should include 
orthophosphate or hexametaphosphate (as PO4) at 40 to 60 ppm, and 
tolyltriazole (active) at 10 to 20 ppm. 
5-7.3.2.2 
Pre-operational Cleaning Procedure. 
If the system passes hydrostatic testing, proceed immediately to this pre-operational 
cleaning and passivation procedure. Do not allow untreated water to be added to the 
system. 
a. Drain and flush any debris from hydrostatic testing. 
b. Dose and circulate (for 24 hours) a sufficient amount of a cleaning formula 
based on the volume of the system. A formulation is provided below. 
c. Drain and flush the system, and clean all strainers. 
d. Fill the system with makeup water and circulate for 30 minutes. 
e. Take a sample of system water while it is circulating. The sample should 
match the makeup water supply for clarity and SS; conductivity ±10 percent; 
and pH ±0.3 pH units from 7.5 to 8.5. 
If necessary, repeat steps a) through e) until the system water matches this description. 
The system should now be clean and passivated. 
5-7.3.2.3 
Chemical Cleaning and Passivation Formulation. 
Apply this chemical cleaning and passivation formulation when the water system pH is 
7.5 to 8.5; adjust pH as required. Formulation limitations may require adding separate 
components to keep things in solution. Other formulations may be used.

Supplemental corrosion inhibitors may be used in conjunction with the phosphate but

CHAPTER 10 CHEMICAL CLEANING OF WATER SYSTEMS 
10-1 
GENERAL GUIDANCE. 
Chemical cleaning of water systems can be divided into two classifications: pre-
operational and remedial. Pre-operational cleaning is performed to prepare the water-
contacted metal surfaces to receive chemical treatment, which provides protection from 
scale, corrosion, and microbiological growth. Remedial cleaning is performed to restore 
water systems that have been fouled with scale, corrosion products, and microbiological 
growth due to inadequate or ineffective water treatment. Cleaning, particularly remedial 
cleaning, is often performed by outside contractors familiar with cleaning procedures, 
techniques, and safety. It should be noted that if the water system is significantly scaled, 
the chemical treatment program was obviously inadequate and was not properly 
designed, set-up, controlled, or applied. After cleaning has been completed, the 
chemical treatment program and QC program must be improved so the same problem 
does not recur. Use of a well-designed QA program would have produced identification 
and notification of potential and developing problems before they became serious. Pre-
operational cleaning is often performed by contractors responsible for the fabrication of 
the water system before turning it over to the military installation. Water system 
operations personnel must assess the effectiveness of any cleaning process that has 
been performed. 
10-1.1 
Pre-Operational Cleaning. 
Pre-operational cleaning can be performed on all new systems or pieces of equipment 
installed in any existing system, including new boiler tubes or new chiller copper tube 
bundles. New piping and coils will usually be contaminated with materials such as mill 
scale, rust, oil, and grease resulting from the fabrication, storage, and installation of the 
equipment. Pre-operational cleaning is performed to remove these materials and 
prepare metal surfaces to receive corrosion protection from chemical treatment. Pre-
operational cleaning agents that are used include detergents, wetting agents, rust 
removers, and dispersants. These cleaning agents have a pH in the range of 9 to 11. 
Water systems containing piping or components constructed of galvanized steel and 
aluminum should not be subjected to procedures that require high pH (greater than 8.5) 
because this would contribute to initiating corrosion of these surfaces. 
The requirement for performing a pre-operational cleaning process is usually written into 
the specification for new construction of a water system that must be performed by a 
mechanical contractor. The mechanical contractor is required to perform the work as 
directed in the specifications; however, if the specifications are not appropriate for the 
specific system, including consideration of all system metallurgy, the cleaning process 
may contribute to corrosion to mild steel, galvanized steel, copper, or aluminum, or it 
may result in incomplete cleaning of dirty and corroded metal surfaces. The 
specifications should be reviewed by a qualified base inspector or qualified independent 
consultant to ensure that cleaning agents and procedures have been specified 
appropriately. A contracting officer or other individual responsible for QA should inspect 
the equipment after cleaning and document the effectiveness of the cleaning process. 


--- page 218 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
196 
10-1.2 
Remedial Cleaning. 
Remedial cleaning is performed to restore a water system that is fouled with scale, 
corrosion products, or microbiological biomass due to inadequate or ineffective water 
treatment. The problem could have resulted from using improper chemical technology, 
failure to maintain treatment levels within control parameters, or the failure of pre-
treatment equipment. The cleaning agents used for remedial cleaning usually include 
acids, chelants, neutralizing agents, and specialty cleaning chemicals. 
10-1.2.1 
Safety and Environmental Issues. 
Remedial cleaning may pose safety issues for personnel handling acids, caustics, and 
various chemicals. There could also be environmental concerns associated with 
chemical disposal. Inexperienced personnel should not perform the chemical cleaning of 
an industrial water system. 
10-1.2.2 
Contracting Cleaning Services. 
For some cleaning jobs, such as large boilers and cooling towers, it may be advisable to 
engage a service company specializing in chemical cleaning. If the cleaning service is 
contracted, it is vital that adequate lines of communication be established, and that 
safety procedures employed by the service company comply with military regulations. 
An orientation meeting should be scheduled between military installation personnel and 
the service company representatives. At that time, the scope of the work can be 
defined, proper procedures initiated, and the nature of the hazards described 
thoroughly. The use of proprietary cleaning chemicals or chemical formulations may be 
involved; disclosure of the use and nature of these chemicals should be made at the 
orientation meeting. Military policies and restrictions can also be explained. The 
inspection of equipment after cleaning is usually the final step in the overall cleaning 
process. 
10-1.3 
Reasons for Cleaning. 
Maintenance of an effective water treatment program is essential to minimize scale and 
corrosion problems in industrial water systems; however, scale and deposits that form 
will require remedial cleaning (descaling). If not removed, these scale and water-caused 
deposits may impact the safety of operations personnel, interfere with heat transfer, and 
cause excessive damage to, or destruction of, the water-using equipment. Cleaning is 
not appropriate for the removal of deposits when corrosion of the system has advanced 
to the point where a large number of leaks may result from the removal of the deposits. 
10-1.4 
Types of Deposits. 
The deposits that occur in water systems can be inorganic mineral salts and corrosion 
products or organic (oily) or biological in nature. Deposits range in composition from 
very dense crystalline structures, to very porous and loosely bound materials, to 
gelatinous slimes. Most of the deposits formed from water constituents consist of 
corrosion products such as iron and copper oxides, mineral scales, or mixtures of these 
materials. 


--- page 219 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
197 
10-1.4.1 
Waterside Deposits Located in Heat Exchangers. 
Water deposits located in heat exchangers are usually carbonate-based scales, while 
steamside deposits may be a mixture of metallic oxides and organic residuals from 
lubricating oil, particularly where reciprocating-type engines are used. In steam 
systems, the oxides are usually iron and copper, resulting from aggressive condensate. 
Microbiological deposits may form in cooling systems from bacterial or algae growths, or 
from decomposition products of various microorganisms. 
10-1.4.2 
Boiler Deposits. 
Boiler deposits may take various forms. In low-pressure boilers using a relatively hard 
feedwater, deposits are essentially calcium and magnesium, silicates, sulfates, 
carbonates, phosphates and hydroxides, plus some organics. Deposits may also 
contain considerable amounts of silica, iron, and copper. These deposits can be spongy 
or porous or relatively hard and glass-like. Deposits of the latter characteristic occur 
where silica is present in appreciable quantities in the boiler water. Deposits in medium-
pressure to high-pressure boiler systems usually are mixtures of iron and copper oxides 
and phosphates. Dense deposits may tend to form in high-heat transfer areas. 
Considerable quantities of sludge-type accumulations may be found in downcomers, 
mud drums, waterwall headers, crossover tubes, and areas of low water circulation in 
the boiler. 
10-2 
REMEDIAL CLEANING PROCEDURES. 
Cleaning procedure information and procedures presented in this Chapter are general 
in nature and must be modified to fit specific applications. Because contractors perform 
most cleanings, these procedures are provided only for general information (see 
paragraphs 10-1.1 and 10-1.2). 
10-2.1 
Cleaning Methods. 
10-2.1.1 
Mechanical Methods. 
Mechanical methods are the oldest techniques used for removing deposits. To perform 
an adequate mechanical-type cleaning, the equipment to be cleaned may need to be 
partially or entirely dismantled. Even when equipment is dismantled, some areas may 
be extremely difficult to reach and clean. Chemical cleaning has largely replaced 
mechanical process equipment cleaning as the most satisfactory method of removing 
deposits; however, mechanical methods such as wire brushing, tumbling, scraping, and 
abrasive blasting with sand and grit are still employed in special applications. 
10-2.1.2 
Cleaning Agents. 
Cleaning agents may be broadly classified as being acid, alkaline, organic, or solvent 
cleaners. There is no general or universal cleaner that removes all deposits. The 
selection of a solvent or cleaning agent is based on the material's ability to remove or 
dissolve the deposit, as well as on cost considerations, safety hazards, and the effect of 
the cleaning material on the metals involved.

5-7.4.1 
Wet Layup of Cooling Water Systems and Equipment. 
Systems and system equipment such as heat exchangers, chiller tube bundles and the 
like can be laid up wet, but first they require a physical cleaning to remove all suspended 
materials. Apply corrosion inhibitors at increased dosages, usually at a level of about 4 
to 5 times the normal maintenance dosage. Apply an increased dosage (within EPA

limits) of a non-oxidizing biocide that has a long half-life, such as glutaraldehyde or 
isothiazolone. 
5-7.4.2 
Dry Layup of Cooling Water Systems and Equipment. 
Systems and equipment can be laid up dry, although dry layup is more appropriate for a 
single piece of equipment, such as a chiller’s condenser tube bundle or other heat 
exchanger. All metal surfaces must be completely dry; residual moisture is not 
acceptable. In humid climates you should use a desiccant such as a quicklime gel or an 
equivalent. Place the desiccant in as many locations as necessary and replace as 
required.

5-3.6 
Cooling Water Fouling. 
The term “fouling” refers to the deposition of materials that are normally held in 
suspension in the cooling water: mud, silt, and other SS brought into the system with 
the makeup water; dust, dirt, and debris scrubbed out of the air passing through the 
tower; product leakage such as oils; corrosion products from the system; and biological 
organisms, both living and dead. Combinations of any or all of these materials can be 
present in the cooling water. 
5-3.7 
Fouling Control. 
Fouling from mud, dirt, and corrosion products can be controlled by the addition of a 
water-soluble polymer dispersant, such as a polyacrylate. The addition of about 4 to 5 
ppm of active polymer, together with sufficient water velocity (3.28 feet per second (1 
meter per second)), can keep foulants in suspension and prevent them from being 
deposited on heat transfer surfaces. Higher dosages (5 to 20 ppm) of active polymer 
can be required for heavily fouled systems. It is best to reduce the loading of SS by 
mechanically removing them from the system through blowdown, filtration, and physical 
sump cleaning. Removing oil or oily materials requires a non-foaming surfactant. 
Paragraph 5-4 describes prevention of fouling by biological organisms. Table 5-2 
summarizes foulant control methods.

# Method of Procedure - PCW cleaning, flushing, passivation and turnover

**Project:** Tull Creek Data Hall - Process Cooling Water (PCW) loop  
**Document:** MOP and design basis for Section 23 25 16 (Rev 3, 2026-07-14)  
**Contractor:** flushing contractor (commissioning engineer of record)  
**Turnover milestone:** TM-4, day 47 from mobilisation (CX-01 Rev B); last programmed activity finishes at hour 721.4 (day 30.1)

**Summary of the programme.** Eight circuits, C1 to C8; total programme cost **$62,484**; 623,234 gal of water drawn (peak day 79,585 gal against the 92,000 gal daily limit); 538,725 gal of effluent, of which 495,632 gal to the metered manhole MH-14 (0.9 per cent below the 500,000 gal authorisation) and 43,093 gal by vacuum tanker; two rented skids and two crews; chemical cleaning complete on day 15 (TM-2 is day 22), film formation complete on day 29 (TM-3 is day 44) and turnover complete on day 30, inside TM-4 at day 47. Every circuit passes every one of its constraint families; section 7 states, per circuit, which constraint has the least room and how much.

## 1. Purpose and scope

This MOP is the design basis and the execution narrative for the pre-operational cleaning,
flushing, chemical cleaning, rinsing, passivation and turnover of the eight tie-in-bounded PCW
circuits C1 to C8, and it discharges the obligations of Section 23 25 16 cl.1.6. It is issued
with the flush plan (`flush_plan.csv`), chemistry plan (`chemistry_plan.csv`), acceptance matrix
(`acceptance_matrix.csv`), schedule (`schedule.csv`), resource and cost statement
(`resources.json`) and constraint register (`constraint_register.csv`). Every figure in this
document is taken from those files; where a figure is recomputed the source is named.

Scope boundary: the hydrostatic test pump, the portable holding tank used to move a cascaded
displacement between tie-ins and the fine filtration below the VD-05 strainer (380 micron) that
CP-311, CP-321 and CP-331 would require at 50 micron are Contractor scope within the lump-sum
mobilisation; they carry no price line in the cost statement (Section 23 25 16 cl.3.10 f).

## 2. Governing documents and document status

## 3. Circuit definition and physical basis

V_f is pipework - the inside area of each line at its M-601 inside diameter times the developed
length of one leg times the number of parallel legs - plus the hold-up of components that are NOT
bypassed. V_s adds the hold-up of every component whether bypassed or not (Section 23 25 16
cl.3.4, cl.3.6).

The Fittings and Valves Sum L/D column of M-601 is NOT added to the pipe volume. M-601 Note 3
states that the column is "for use with the equivalent-length method", that is for the friction
head of cl.3.2 c, and an equivalent length represents the fitting pressure loss, not the volume
the fitting displaces. Adding it would overstate the water in C1 by 3,990 gal (12 %) and in C3 by
1,172 gal (19 %) and would overstate every dose, rinse and effluent figure in the programme.
Judgement call 14 in section 9A records the choice.

## 4. Hydraulic design basis

All hydraulic quantities follow Section 23 25 16 cl.3.2 and DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 Vol. 3 with
rho = 62.30 lbm/ft3, nu = 1.08e-5 ft2/s, Colebrook-White friction factor with the absolute
roughness of Section 23 21 16 cl.2.2 (carbon steel 0.00015 ft, galvanized 0.0005 ft, copper
0.000005 ft, hose 0.0008 ft), and the equivalent length method with sum L/D from M-601.

### 4.1 Flushing flow

The flushing flow is the flow that gives, in every leg of every line, the greater of the UFC
3-230-13 foulant-suspension velocity (3.28 ft/s, 5-3.7) and the project class minimum of
Section 23 25 16 cl.3.3 b: 4.0 ft/s for a circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a
cold-plate device, 2.0 ft/s otherwise. The governing line is the one whose legs x A is largest,
because it carries the lowest leg velocity; a 3 % design reserve is applied above the criterion
so that rounding in the field record cannot take the circuit below it.

The same flow is maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and
every rinse displacement (cl.3.3), and it is the flow at which the passivation charge and the
turnover fill are circulated.

### 4.2 Required head and skid duty

Required head = static lift + friction of the MAIN circulation path (the single-leg lines of
M-601 at the total circuit flow) + the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path
scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 + the temporary hose loss and the VD-05 strainer loss at the
skid's own share of the flow. Where a skid combination is used, the units are in parallel, share
the flow equally, and each must develop the required head at its own flow (cl.3.2 d and e).

| C1 | FS-1200-A | 1 | 1216.9 | 92.0 | 114.0 | 0.81 | inside published curve (last point 1400 gpm) |
| C2 | FS-1200-A | 1 | 642.4 | 50.4 | 183.9 | 0.27 | inside published curve (last point 1400 gpm) |
| C3 | FS-1200-A | 1 | 742.0 | 58.7 | 174.3 | 0.34 | inside published curve (last point 1400 gpm) |
| C4 | FS-600-A | 1 | 371.0 | 101.9 | 152.6 | 0.67 | inside published curve (last point 700 gpm) |
| C5 | FS-1200-A | 1 | 490.4 | 83.5 | 193.8 | 0.43 | inside published curve (last point 1400 gpm) |
| C6 | FS-600-A | 1 | 371.0 | 105.2 | 152.6 | 0.69 | inside published curve (last point 700 gpm) |
| C7 | FS-600-A | 1 | 304.2 | 109.2 | 162.4 | 0.67 | inside published curve (last point 700 gpm) |

4.026 in. hose supplied with an FS-600 loses 80 ft w.c. at 600 gpm, so a single FS-600 cannot
serve the four high-flow circuits; C1 is beyond the FS-600 curve and needs the FS-1200, and
C2, C3 and C5 need either the FS-1200 or both FS-600s in parallel. The FS-1200 has been assigned
to C1, C2, C3 and C5 so that no circuit depends on both FS-600 units at once and the FS-600-A
can work the four small circuits concurrently.

### 4.3 Components in the flushed path

Every component shown in M-602 with a full-size temporary bypass spool is bypassed for the
initial flush and the chemical cleaning (cl.3.4): HX-201A, HX-201B, CDU-301, CP-311, CDU-302,
CP-321, CP-331 and CL-401. The components that stay in the path are checked at the declared flow:

| Component | Circuit | dP at declared flow (ft w.c.) | Max allowable dP (ft w.c.) | Temperature (degF) | Max particle size (micron) | Result |

| BT-101 | C1 | 0.00 | 15 | 68 <= 200 | 380 <= 800 | pass |

(M-602 Notes 1 and 5); the max allowable figures against them are mechanical ratings, not
flushing limits. ST-601 has no bypass: at the C8 declared flow of 155.7 gpm its drop is 10.1 ft w.c. against
a 25 ft w.c. limit (40 % of it), and it is a full-bore vessel that passes the 380 micron
strainer opening.

## 5. Chemistry design basis

### 5.1 Makeup water (SW-02)

pH 7.6; conductivity 615 microS/cm; total hardness 288 mg/L as CaCO3; chloride 505 mg/L;
sulphate 355 mg/L; silica 11 mg/L as SiO2; iron 0.09 mg/L; TSS < 1 mg/L.

### 5.2 Programme selection

C1, C2, C3, C4, C5 and C7 - molybdate-azole. C6 - polysilicate-azole, because the circuit
contains the aluminium cold-plate bank CP-331 and UFC 3-230-13 6-2.2.5 states that the
polysilicate programme "is especially beneficial when aluminum metal is present", which is what
VD-04 chemical compatibility note 1 requires. C8 - polysilicate-azole, because the circuit is
hot-dip galvanized (RFI-022) and UFC 5-7.3.1 limits the pH to 8.5 during cleaning and
passivation, which the molybdate band (pH 8.5 to 9.5 in service) cannot guarantee.

On C1, C2 and C3 no copper is wetted anywhere, so no azole is carried: UFC 6-2.2.3 step 4
requires the 10 ppm tolyltriazole only if copper is present. The programme is still the
molybdate-azole programme, dosed with MO-500 alone.

The nitrite programmes are excluded by the makeup analysis: chloride + sulphate = 505 + 355 =
860 mg/L exceeds the 800 mg/L limit of UFC 6-2.2.2 and the (NO2 + Mo) - 100 = 250 mg/L limit of
6-2.2.4. NB-700 is therefore not ordered.

### 5.3 Chemical cleaning

The cleaning product is dosed volumetrically on the SYSTEM volume at the VD-06 application rate
(cl.3.4, VD-06 Note 4a): CL-100 at 1.5 gal per 1,000 gal for the carbon-steel circuits and CL-210
at 2.0 gal per 1,000 gal for the galvanized and aluminium circuits C6 and C8. A target residual
does not apply to a cleaning row. The polyacrylate dispersant PD-45 is carried with the cleaning
charge at 4 ppm active polymer (UFC 5-3.7, together with the 3.28 ft/s velocity). The charge is
circulated for 24 h of OCCUPIED time per circuit (UFC 5-7.3.2.2 b), scheduled as a single 24 h
activity so that the sum of the stage hours is the contact time.

### 5.4 Rinse

C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n) with C_mk = 615 microS/cm and C_0 = 2,600 microS/cm for
CL-100 / 2,150 microS/cm for CL-210 (VD-06 Note 3); eta = 0.45 where the circuit contains a
cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank (C4, C5, C6, C7) and 0.62 otherwise (C1, C2, C3, C8).
The acceptance criterion is the UFC 5-7.3.2.2 e one: conductivity within +/-10 % of makeup,
i.e. <= 676.5 microS/cm, and pH within +/-0.3 of 7.6 clipped to the 7.5 to 8.5 window, i.e. a
control band of 7.5 to 7.9 that satisfies both permitted readings of the criterion.

| C2 | CL-100 | 2600 | 0.62 | 6 | 27980 | 27980 | 663.1 | 0.020 |

### 5.5 Passivation and turnover

The passivation tables of UFC 3-230-13 (Tables 5-14 and 5-15, the tables the document identifies
for passivation) give 40-60 ppm as Mo and 40-50 ppm as SiO2 at pH 7.5-8.5 with 14-21 days of
film formation, and 10-20 ppm as TTA at pH 6.5-7.9. The programme is dosed at the bottom of the
band (40 ppm) and held for the bottom of the film-formation range (14 days = 336 occupied hours).
Where copper is wetted (C4, C5, C6, C7) the azole is carried at 10 ppm and the passivation pH is
controlled to the intersection of the molybdate/silicate band and the TTA band, 7.5 to 7.9.

Turnover uses RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP for every circuit. That method is permitted because for both
selected programmes the maintenance residual of the programme paragraph is above the passivation
residual: molybdate 100-125 ppm (UFC 6-2.2.3) against 40-60 ppm passivation, and polysilicate
80-100 ppm (UFC 6-2.2.5) against 40-50 ppm passivation, while the azole is held at 10 ppm in both.
The retained charge is therefore raised, not diluted, by the top-up. The top-up is drawn through
the SV-2 softener (C-101) and is dosed only with the increment between the maintenance and
passivation residuals, on the SYSTEM volume (Section 23 25 16 cl.3.8 reporting convention).

### 5.6 Chemical quantities and orders

Every dosing row is rounded up to whole packages at the VD-06 package price, with no pooling
across stages or circuits (cl.3.10 e). The order dates in `resources.json` are the first use day
less the VD-06 lead time; MO-500 (21 days) must be ordered 21 days before mobilisation.

## 9. Defects found in the documents

1. Four hydrostatic test charts cited by CX-02 (TR-0414, TR-0416, TR-0417, TR-0418) are missing
   from the commissioning record. Four circuits therefore have to be retested, which is extra
   scope created by a record deficiency, not by the work.
2. The superseded M-PID-103 Rev A and the superseded SW-03 Rev A remain in the issued document
   set alongside their current revisions; both were located and excluded, but they are a live
   risk of a wrong line assignment or a wrong discharge limit being used by others.
3. UFC 3-230-13 Table 5-14 contains typographical unit errors: "20-30 days as PO4" and
   "10-20 days as TTA" should read ppm. Read as ppm (as Table 5-15 and the surrounding text
   confirm); the error does not affect the molybdate and polysilicate lines used here.
4. The site softener SF-1 is undersized for construction use: at the SW-02 hardness of 288 mg/L
   its 88,000 grain capacity yields only 5,225 gal per daily regeneration, about 0.8 % of the
   programme draw. It cannot deliver the Table 6-1 makeup quality for a campaign of this size.
   Consequence recorded for the owner: the final fill is softened through SV-2 within that
   capacity, but the water retained in the RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP circuits is rinse water at the raw
   hardness of 288 mg/L, above the 250 mg/L of Table 6-1. To bring the operating system inside
   Table 6-1 the owner must drain and refill each circuit with softened water, or soften the
   makeup over a longer period, once the softener can supply the volume; this is outside the
   flushing campaign and is flagged as a hand-over action in section 11A.
5. The FS-600 skid is supplied with a 4.026 in. hose: at 600 gpm the 300 ft run alone loses
   about 80 ft w.c., so the published 106 ft w.c. at 600 gpm is almost entirely consumed by the
   hose. The datasheet does not say so, and a plan built on the pump curve alone would fail on
   site. This is why C2, C3 and C5 are assigned to the FS-1200.
6. VD-06 quotes no density or active content for CL-100 and CL-210. That is correct for a
   volumetric product (Note 4a), but it means the cleaning dose cannot be expressed as a mass and
   must not be entered as a target residual.
7. M-601 does not assign lines to circuits and M-603 does not list lines; the circuit definition
   exists only on the P&ID sheets. A reader who works from the schedules alone will mis-size C4
   and C5.

## 10. Execution narrative

**Mobilisation (hour 0).** TM-0. FS-600-A and FS-600-B delivered (SI-05). Temporary power
energised at the tie-in panels of SW-04. Spill containment, eyewash and the SDS pack (VD-07)
placed at the dosing point. Strainers, bypass spools and hoses checked against VD-05 and M-602.

**Hydrostatic testing.** C3, C5, C6 and C7 are tested at 127.5 psig for 120 minutes with the
Contractor's test pump (not a flush skid, Section 23 25 16 cl.3.10 f) before any chemical
cleaning; the 127.5 psig is below the 150 psig rating of the hose and strainer that remain in
the assembled circuit (VD-05 note 1, M-602 Note 3). A signed chart is filed for each, which is
what CX-02 lacked. C1, C2, C4 and C8 are not retested (Section 23 21 16 cl.3.3).

**Initial flush.** One full circuit displacement at the declared flow with the bypass spools
fitted and the 380 micron strainer in the skid discharge. The lowest-velocity segment is recorded
(CX-03 item 2) and the strainer is cleaned at every drain.

**Chemical cleaning.** The cleaning charge is made up on the SYSTEM volume with the dispersant,
circulated for 24 h, then drained. Spent solutions from C4, C5, C6, C7 and C8 are hauled; the
carbon-steel circuits C1, C2 and C3 are sewered after confirming pH 8.4 and no copper or zinc
(VD-06 Note 3). Strainers are cleaned at the drain. Because SW-03 also sets a 300 mg/L total
suspended solids limit that VD-06 does not characterise, every initial-flush and spent-cleaning
stream is sampled for TSS before the drain valve is opened; a stream above 300 mg/L is diverted
to the tanker under the RFI-031 contingency instead of to MH-14, and the diversion is recorded
in the log with its volume, route, pH and temperature.

**Rinse.** n displacements at the declared flow, with the cascade arrangement C1 to C5, C5 to C3,
C3 to C2 and C8 to C7. Each cascade moves exactly one receiver displacement volume out of the
donor's final rinse effluent into a portable holding tank and then into the receiver, so no
circuit receives more than one cascaded displacement and no donor FLUSH volume is smaller than
its receiver's. Rinse samples (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity, pH) are taken while
circulating at every displacement and logged on CX-03 item 6. The circuit is left FULL after the
last displacement.

**Passivation.** The charge is dosed into the standing water on the SYSTEM volume, pH adjusted
into the band, and circulated; the residual and pH at the start of film formation are recorded
(CX-03 item 7). The skid is then released and the circuit is held, unattended, for 14 days
(336 h, CX-03 item 8). No skid and no crew is charged during the hold.

**Turnover.** TM-3 is met when the last film-formation hold closes (day 29, inside
the contractual day 44 milestone). Each circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with softened water
carrying the maintenance charge, recirculated for 30 minutes and sampled while circulating for
the maintenance residual, the azole residual and the total aerobic bacteria count. Strainers are
removed at TM-4 (CX-03 item 11), at the start of the turnover fill. Turnover is complete at hour 721, day 30, inside TM-4.

**Records.** The CX-03 log is maintained for every circuit with the minimum velocity and its
segment, the strainer mesh and removal milestone, the cleaning circulation time, the rinse
results against makeup, the passivation residual/pH/hold and every discharge event with volume,
route, pH and temperature. The acceptance matrix in `acceptance_matrix.csv` states the gate, the
sense and the numeric threshold with the document and clause for every parameter the turnover
log must carry (Section 23 25 16 cl.1.5 a to d).

## 1. BLOCKING — Cu-bearing circuits cannot meet the turnover azole residual: no azole is dosed at FINAL_FILL and the retained charge is diluted below 10 ppm

**Requirement.** Section 23 25 16 cl.3.5: “Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry
the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.” UFC 3-230-13 6-2.2.3
step 4: “If copper is present, maintain a minimum of 10 ppm of tolyltriazole.” Section 23 25 16
cl.1.5 d requires the TURNOVER gate to carry the maintenance inhibitor residual to the limit of
the governing document.

**What the deliverable has.** `chemistry_plan.csv` has TA-90 only on PASSIVATE rows for C4, C5,
C6, C7 (10 ppm). There is no TA-90 row on FINAL_FILL for any of them, and `chemical_orders` orders
only 4 × 1-gal TA-90 bottles, exactly the four passivation rows.

**What it should be.** The destroyed/removed azole must be replaced in the top-up water (or
directly) so the circuit is at ≥10 ppm TTA at turnover. Because the retained passivation charge is
at 10 ppm in the FLUSH volume and the top-up is un-azolated, the final concentration is:

- C4: 10 × 5,956.6 / 8,536.6 = **6.98 ppm**
- C5: 10 × 6,405.8 / 8,985.8 = **7.13 ppm**
- C6: 10 × 4,227.1 / 5,677.1 = **7.45 ppm**
- C7: 10 × 4,086.0 / 6,036.0 = **6.77 ppm**

All are below the 10 ppm lower limit. The dose needed on the FINAL_FILL top-up is 0.048 gal
(C4), 0.048 gal (C5), 0.027 gal (C6) and 0.037 gal (C7), i.e. one 1-gal TA-90 bottle each;
`packages` and `chemical_orders` should be 8 bottles total, not 4. The acceptance matrix itself
(`C4..C7, TURNOVER, maintenance azole residual, lower limit 10 ppm`) therefore cannot be met by
the plan as written.

**Evidence.** `submission.zip!chemistry_plan.csv` rows C4/C5/C6/C7 FINAL_FILL (only MO-500/PS-330);
`submission.zip!resources.json` `chemical_orders` TA-90 packages = 4; computed final concentrations
above from the Vf/Vs values in `MOP.md` section 3 and `flush_plan.csv`.

## 2. BLOCKING — Components returned to the path at PASSIVATE/FINAL_FILL exceed their maximum allowable pressure drop (M-602) and, for C4–C7, the skid cannot deliver the declared flow

**Requirement.** M-602 Note 2: “Max Allowable Pressure Drop is the limit the component may be
operated to at any flow, including temporary flushing flows.” Section 23 25 16 cl.3.2 d: required
head includes “the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as
dP_rated × (Q/Q_rated)²”. Section 23 25 16 cl.3.4: a component left in the flushed path must be
within its maximum allowable pressure drop.

**What the deliverable has.** `flush_plan.csv` `protection` on PASSIVATE/FINAL_FILL says “Bypass
spools removed after chemical cleaning” for C2–C7, so HX-201A/B, CDU-301/302, CP-311/321/331 and
CL-401 are back in the pumped path. But `required_head_ft` and `flow_gpm` on those rows are the
same as the flushing rows (C4 371 gpm/101.9 ft, C5 490.4/83.5, C6 371/105.2, C7 304.2/109.2,
C3 742/58.7), i.e. the component pressure drops are not included. MOP §4.3 only checks PMP-101,
BT-101 and ST-601, the components that stay in the path during initial flush/chemical cleaning.

**What it should be.** At the declared flows the component drops are:

| Circuit | Component | dP at declared flow (ft) | Max allowable (ft) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C3 | HX-201B (46 at 610 gpm) | 46×(742/610)² = **68.1** | 58 | exceeds by 10.1 ft |
| C4 | CDU-301 (38 at 380) | 36.2 | 48 | within |
| C4 | CP-311 (52 at 380) | 49.6 | 65 | within |
| C5 | CDU-302 (38 at 360) | 38×(490.4/360)² = **70.5** | 48 | exceeds by 22.5 ft |
| C5 | CP-321 (52 at 360) | 52×(490.4/360)² = **96.5** | 65 | exceeds by 31.5 ft |
| C6 | CP-331 (58 at 300) | 58×(371/300)² = **88.7** | 72 | exceeds by 16.7 ft |
| C7 | CL-401 (41 at 250) | 41×(304.2/250)² = **60.7** | 52 | exceeds by 8.7 ft |

Required head including components and my independent cl.3.2 d base values: C4 89.3+85.8 =
**175.1 ft** vs FS-600-A available **152.6 ft**; C5 79.4+167.0 = **246.4 ft** vs FS-1200-A
**193.8 ft**; C6 92.2+88.7 = **180.9 ft** vs FS-600-A **152.6 ft**; C7 101.0+60.7 = **161.7 ft**
vs FS-600-A **162.4 ft** (0.4 % — at the limit); C3 56.0+68.1 = **124.1 ft** vs FS-1200-A
**174.3 ft** (head okay, component limit not). C4–C6 therefore cannot circulate at the declared flow with the bypasses removed; C7 is at the head limit (161.7 vs 162.4 ft, 0.4 %) but still exceeds its component maximum; C3, C5, C6 and C7 exceed a component maximum. The plan must either
keep the components bypassed (and passivate them another way) or reduce the passivation/turnover
circulation flow to a value at which every component is inside its max dP and the skid can deliver
the head, and recompute the stage durations at that lower flow. The MOP’s `GOVERNING CONSTRAINT`
lines and head margins do not reflect this.

**Evidence.** `submission.zip!flush_plan.csv` PASSIVATE/FINAL_FILL rows (`protection`, flow,
required_head, skid_head_avail); `submission.zip!MOP.md` §4.3 and §5.5; M-602 rows HX-201B,
CDU-301/302, CP-311/321/331, CL-401; VD-01/VD-02 curves. Computations above use

## 3. BLOCKING — Discharge of the first rinse displacements from copper/zinc circuits to MH-14 violates the SW-03 local limits

**Requirement.** Section 23 25 16 cl.3.7: “Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions
of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which
SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.” SW-03 Rev B §3
local limits: copper 1.0 mg/L, zinc 1.0 mg/L.

**What the deliverable has.** `flush_plan.csv` routes every `DRAIN_RINSE` for C4, C5, C6, C7 and C8
to `SEWER`. Only the `CHEM_CLEAN` rows of those circuits are `HAUL` (plus C6/C7 hydro and initial
flush). The spent cleaning solution is characterised by VD-06 Note 3 as 3.4 mg/L Cu for CL-100
(C4, C5, C7), 1.6 mg/L Cu for CL-210 (C6), and 5.5 mg/L Zn for CL-210 on galvanised (C8).

**What it should be.** The rinse starts at the spent-solution concentration and decays with the
displacement model; the first displacements are above the local limit and must be tankered:

- C4/C5/C7 (Cu 3.4, η 0.45): after 1 displacement 2.17 mg/L, after 2 1.38, after 3 0.88 → at

- C6 (Cu 1.6, η 0.45): after 1 1.02 mg/L → at least the first displacement exceeds 1.0.
- C8 (Zn 5.5, η 0.62): after 1 2.96, after 2 1.59, after 3 0.86 → at least the first two exceed 1.0.

The plan therefore sewers roughly 49,000 gal of non-compliant rinse (C4/C5/C7 2×Vf each = 32,897
gal, C6 4,227 gal, C8 2×5,791 = 11,582 gal) that should be hauled. The sewer total would fall
from 495,632 gal to about 447,000 gal, still below the 500,000 gal cap, so the cap is not a
justification. The MOP §11.9 itself says “the copper- and zinc-bearing streams … go by tanker”,
but the plan’s routes do not do so for the rinse.

**Evidence.** `submission.zip!flush_plan.csv` DRAIN_RINSE rows C4–C8 (`discharge_route`);

## 5. MAJOR — Rinse endpoint for cascaded circuits is computed with makeup conductivity, not the donor’s final rinse quality; if the cascade is the last displacement the circuit fails 676.5 µS/cm

**Requirement.** Section 23 25 16 cl.3.6: “A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent
of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A
cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement.” The displacement model C_n = C_mk +
(C_0 − C_mk) exp(−η n) uses C_mk, the makeup conductivity; a cascade displacement is not makeup.

**What the deliverable has.** `flush_plan.csv` C5 `CASCADE_FROM:C1`, C3 `CASCADE_FROM:C5`,
C2 `CASCADE_FROM:C3`, C7 `CASCADE_FROM:C8`; `MOP.md` §5.4 reports C_n = 663.1 / 669.2 / 663.1 /
652.2, i.e. the all-makeup model. The plan does not state where in the displacement sequence the
cascade falls. `schedule.csv` has one `DRAIN_RINSE` activity per receiver, so the order is not
fixed.

**What it should be.** The donor final rinse conductivities are C1 663.1, C5 669.2, C3 663.1,
C8 652.2 µS/cm, all above the 615 µS/cm makeup. Recomputing the mixing:

| Receiver | donor C | η | n | cascade first | cascade last | limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5 | 663.1 | 0.45 | 8 | 669.98 | **686.67** | 676.5 |
| C3 | 669.2 | 0.62 | 6 | 664.23 | **688.15** | 676.5 |
| C2 | 663.1 | 0.62 | 6 | 664.11 | **685.33** | 676.5 |
| C7 | 652.2 | 0.45 | 8 | 669.82 | **682.72** | 676.5 |

If the cascade is the first displacement, the model is optimistic by 0.6–1.1 µS/cm but passes; if
the cascade is the last displacement, all four receivers fail. The MOP’s §5.4 C_n values and
0.011–0.020 conductivity margins are therefore not the plan’s actual margins; the procedure must
state that the cascade is the first displacement (and the model should use the donor quality), or
the number of displacements must be increased.

**Evidence.** `submission.zip!flush_plan.csv` water_source rows and passes; `MOP.md` §5.4 table;
computed above from C_mk 615, C_0 2,600, η 0.45/0.62 and the donor final C_n from the same table.

"""Build the turnover package: flush_plan, chemistry_plan, acceptance_matrix,
schedule, resources.json, constraint_register, MOP.md"""
import math, os, json, csv
from eng import *

VM = 1.03                      # velocity design margin
CMK = 615.0                    # makeup conductivity SW-02
PH_MK = 7.6
TOWER_RATE = 168.0
SEWER_RATE = 9.40
METER_RATE = 6.20
TRUCK_RATE = 19.80
CREW_RATE = 820.0

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ derived circuit data
CIRC = {}
for cid, c in CIRCUITS.items():
    vreq = max(3.28, c['vclass'])
    Q = 0.0
    for (ln, D, L, legs, sld, mat) in LINES[c['lines']]:
        Q = max(Q, vreq*line_flow_area(D, legs)*GPM_PER_CFS)
    Q = Q*VM
    gov, allv = vel_check(cid, Q)
    vpipe, vf, vs = circuit_volumes(cid)
    n, Cn = n_rinse(c['C0'], c['eta'])
    # candidate skids
    opts = []
    for used in (['FS-600-A'], ['FS-600-A', 'FS-600-B'], ['FS-1200-A']):
        kw = sum(SKIDS[u]['kw'] for u in used)
        if kw > c['kw']:
            continue
        r = circuit_hydraulics(cid, used[0], len(used), Q)
        ha = skid_head(used[0], Q/len(used))
        if ha is None:
            continue
        if r['h_req'] <= ha:
            opts.append((used, r, ha))
    CIRC[cid] = dict(vreq=vreq, Q=round(Q, 1), gov=gov, allv=allv, vf=vf, vs=vs,
                     n=n, Cn=Cn, opts=opts)

# chosen skid per circuit (cost/staging decision, documented in MOP)
ASSIGN = {'C1': ['FS-1200-A'], 'C2': ['FS-1200-A'], 'C3': ['FS-1200-A'],
          'C4': ['FS-600-A'], 'C5': ['FS-1200-A'],
          'C6': ['FS-600-A'], 'C7': ['FS-600-A'], 'C8': ['FS-600-A']}

# cascade plan  donor -> receiver
CASCADE = {'C5': 'C1', 'C3': 'C5', 'C2': 'C3', 'C7': 'C8'}
DONATE = {v: k for k, v in CASCADE.items()}

for cid, d in CIRC.items():
    c = CIRCUITS[cid]
    d['skus'] = ASSIGN[cid]
    d['nskid'] = len(ASSIGN[cid])
    r = circuit_hydraulics(cid, d['skus'][0], d['nskid'], d['Q'])
    d['h'] = r
    d['hav'] = skid_head(d['skus'][0], d['Q']/d['nskid'])
    d['c'] = 1 if cid in CASCADE else 0
    d['don_to'] = DONATE.get(cid)
    d['don_gal'] = CIRC[DONATE[cid]]['vf'] if cid in DONATE else 0.0
    d['rinse_draw'] = (d['n'] - d['c'])*d['vf']
    d['rinse_eff'] = (d['n'] - 1)*d['vf'] - d['don_gal']
    d['t_flush'] = d['vf']/d['Q']*60.0/60.0*60/60  # hours = gal/(gpm*60)
    d['t_flush'] = d['vf']/(d['Q']*60.0)
    d['t_rinse'] = d['n']*d['t_flush']
    d['t_chem'] = max(24.0, d['t_flush'])
    d['t_pass'] = d['t_flush'] + 0.5
    d['t_fill'] = (d['vs']-d['vf'])/(d['Q']*60.0) + 0.5
    d['hydro'] = 0.0 if c['hydro_ok'] else 2.0
    d['draw_hydro'] = 0.0 if c['hydro_ok'] else d['vf']
    d['draw_flush'] = d['vf']
    d['draw_chem'] = d['vf']
    d['draw_fill'] = d['vs'] - d['vf']
    d['program_maint'] = 100.0 if c['cleaner'] == 'CL-100' else 80.0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    tot = 0
    for cid, d in CIRC.items():
        print('%s Q=%7.1f gov=%s vf=%6.0f vs=%6.0f n=%d skus=%s req=%6.1f hav=%6.1f '
              'm=%.3f t_f=%.3f t_r=%.2f' % (cid, d['Q'], d['gov'][0], d['vf'], d['vs'],
              d['n'], '+'.join(d['skus']), d['h']['h_req'], d['hav'],
              (d['hav']-d['h']['h_req'])/d['hav'], d['t_flush'], d['t_rinse']))
        w = d['draw_hydro']+d['draw_flush']+d['draw_chem']+d['rinse_draw']+d['draw_fill']
        e = d['draw_hydro']+d['draw_flush']+d['draw_chem']+d['rinse_eff']
        tot += w
        print('    draw=%8.0f eff=%8.0f  (draw-eff=%.0f vs vs=%.0f)' % (w, e, w-e, d['vs']))
    print('TOTAL DRAW', round(tot))

SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
1.1   SUMMARY
This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
  a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
  b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
  c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
  d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
    GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
       1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
   with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
       h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
  a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
  b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
       C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
       eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
       eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
3.7   DISCHARGE
All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
3.8   TURNOVER
Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
  RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
  DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.
Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
    hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
    initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
    chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
    rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
    passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
    film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
    turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
    turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
3.10   COST BASIS
Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
  a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
  b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each crew-shift between the circuits attended in it IN PROPORTION TO THE ATTENDED HOURS each took inside the shift; the share is a real number and is NOT rounded. A stage's attended hours are spread over the shifts its scheduled activities occupy IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS of those activities in each shift, the same convention cl.3.9 uses for the daily water draw.
     DURATION IS OCCUPIED TIME. A stage lasts as long as its activities OCCUPY: its duration is the SUM of the hours of the activities scheduled for it, and an idle gap between two of them is no part of it. No period this Section requires - a contact time, a circulation time, a displacement at the declared flow, a recirculation, a film-formation hold - is satisfied by an ENVELOPE that merely contains it. Work not done in the gap is not work done. The attended time of a stage is:
       hydrostatic test        the specified hold
       initial flush           n_f x V_f at the declared flow
       chemical cleaning       the greater of the required circulation time and V_f at the declared flow
       rinse                   n_r x V_f at the declared flow
       passivation charge      V_f at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
       turnover                the fill volume of the declared method at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
     An unattended film-formation hold, and unattended standby inside a longer scheduled occupancy, are not charged (SW-01 cl.3, 01 91 13 cl.1.7); a stage with no attended time opens no shift. A crew attends one activity at a time and a rented unit serves one circuit at a time, so no crew may be charged with more than 12 attended hours in a shift and no unit held for more than 24 hours in a day.
     WHAT a AND b MEAN FOR THE PROGRAMME. Both lines are bought by the period, so the two of them price the SEQUENCE, not the circuit: a programme that dovetails its circuits into the same unit-days and the same crew-shifts pays a fraction of what the same engineering costs when the circuits are run one after another. Neither line can be worked out from one circuit in isolation, and a circuit's share of both moves when another circuit's schedule moves. Against that pull stands cl.3.9 and SW-01 cl.2: the site's daily water allocation is shared too, so drawing the whole programme into a few days buys the excess at the trucked rate, and the cascade links of cl.3.6 force the circuits they join to rinse in sequence. The economic plan is the one that settles those against each other.
  c. Water: metered rate up to the daily allocation and the trucked rate above it (SW-01 cl.1, cl.2). APPORTIONMENT: the allocation is a site-wide meter, so form ONE programme-wide average rate - the metered and trucked volumes priced at their own rates, divided by the total volume drawn - and apply that single rate to every circuit's draw. Do not attempt to attribute particular gallons to particular circuits.
  d. Effluent: the sewer rate for volume to the metered connection, the tanker rate for volume remove

Permanent pipework, valves and fittings are rated for 300 psig at 200 degF.

3.3   HYDROSTATIC TESTING
Test each circuit hydrostatically at 1.5 times the system operating pressure of 85 psig, and in no case less than 125 psig, held for not less than 120 minutes with no loss of pressure and no visible leakage.
The test pressure shall not exceed the lowest pressure rating of any component in the circuit under test, including temporary equipment.
Circuits recorded as tested and accepted in CX-02 shall not be retested; retesting an accepted circuit is a change in scope. Any circuit not so recorded shall be tested before chemical cleaning begins.=======

Hydrogen Peroxide. 
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a liquid that is usually used at a concentration of 30 
percent in water. Hydrogen peroxide is considered one of the most environmentally 
friendly oxidizing biocides because it degrades to water; however, concentrated 
hydrogen peroxide will react in a violent manner when it comes into contact with organic 
chemicals and materials.

5-4.4.2 
Non-Oxidizing Biocides. 
Non-oxidizing biocides are microbiocides that act as “poisons;” they disrupt the 
metabolic or reproductive processes of micro- and macro-organisms and are therefore 
toxic. Non-oxidizing biocides are organic compounds that are very toxic to organisms, 
including human beings and animals. They are usually liquids, but some are available 
as dry products (such as pellets, solids). A major consideration for their use is their 
persistence with respect to the discharge limitations for water (effluent) containing these 
toxic substances. Also, when choosing and applying a non-oxidizing biocide, you must 
consider the cooling tower system’s operating parameters, such as pH and retention 
time. The applied dosages of microbiocides should never exceed EPA maximum limits, 
which are always printed on the container labels. The labels will also identify the active 
microbiocide ingredient, the percentage of each chemical that is present in the 


--- page 151 ---

formulation, and the EPA registration number. Control programs often combine both 
oxidizing and non-oxidizing biocides. The most important aspect of bio-fouling control is 
to match the non-oxidizing biocide to the problem organism. Table 5-7 provides 
guidelines for non-oxidizing biocide effectiveness.

5-4.5 
Algae Control. 
Algae can be controlled by two techniques: chemical methods and physical methods. 
Since algae require sunlight to survive and grow, covering the upper hot water decks of 
cooling towers with plywood can often control algae deposits. Chemical methods consist 
of using oxidizing and non-oxidizing biocides, which can control algae to various 
degrees (see Tables 5-6 and 5-7). The effectiveness of oxidizers is considered only fair 
while that of several non-oxidizers is in the range of very good to excellent. One of the 
more effective biocides for algae is terbutylazine, a triazine product (see Table 5-7). 
5-4.6 
Bacterial Control. 
Accepted industry practice for bacterial control is the use of oxidizing and non-oxidizing 
biocides that are specific for the type of bacteria. The most cost-effective microbiocide 
programs for medium and large cooling towers use an oxidizer as a primary biocide and 
one or more non-oxidizers selectively as a secondary biocide (see Tables 5-6 and 5-7). 
Smaller cooling systems often use one or more non- oxidizing biocides, although dry 


--- page 152 ---
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
130 
oxidizing biocides are also used commonly. The most overlooked aspect of bacterial 
control is maintaining a system kept clean of deposits and SS (such as dirt, silt, sand, 
corrosion products) through the use of filters and periodic wash-down procedures. 
Clean systems reduce the demand for chemical and microbiological control. Table 5-8 
shows accepted industry guidelines for a bacterial control program with the use of a test 
kit.
